body.heading: A mountain with a secret underneath
paragraphs: A real volcano is not really a mountain with fire in it — it is a crack in the Earth's crust with a plumbing system: stored molten rock below, a pipe to the surface, and an opening at the top. This model builds that plumbing in cardboard and clay, labels every part, and finishes with an eruption that shows what the pressure does.

body.heading: Meet the parts
paragraphs: The magma chamber — the underground store of molten rock (in the model, a small cup hidden in the cone). The vent — the pipe up the middle that magma travels through. The crater — the bowl-shaped opening at the summit. The cone — the mountain itself, built layer by layer by old eruptions. And lava — the name magma gets once it reaches the surface; in the model, red foam plays the part.

body.heading: You will need
paragraphs: A plastic bottle (a grown-up cuts it down), a tray, cardboard or clay or damp sand for the cone, a small cup for the chamber if you build a cutaway, warm water, bicarbonate of soda, vinegar, washing-up liquid, red and orange food colouring, and labels on sticks or card for the parts.

paragraphs: Step 1 — Build the cone. Stand the cut bottle in the middle of the tray. Mould cardboard, clay or damp sand around it into a mountain, leaving the bottle's mouth open at the summit — that mouth is the crater, and the bottle is the vent.

Step 2 — Label the anatomy. Push label sticks into the cone: CRATER at the top, VENT down the middle, MAGMA CHAMBER at the base, LAVA FLOW where the foam will run. A model you can label is a model you understand.
Step 3 — Charge the chamber. A grown-up pours warm water into the bottle until half full, adds washing-up liquid and red-orange colouring, then two big spoons of bicarbonate of soda.

Step 4 — Eruption. The grown-up pours in half a cup of vinegar and everyone steps back. Foam bursts from the crater and pours down the cone in lava flows. Compare with your labels: the foam took the vent, exited the crater, and became 'lava' the moment it reached the surface — exactly the real journey.

body.heading: The science bit
paragraphs: The model's eruption runs on fizz power: vinegar (an acid) meets bicarbonate of soda (a base) and they react to make carbon dioxide gas — thousands of bubbles that need room, pushing the foam up and out. A real volcano erupts for a cousin of this reason: magma underground holds dissolved gases, and when pressure drops as it rises, the gases rush out as bubbles and drive the eruption. The shapes match too — the model's cone, crater and vent are the real anatomy, and geologists read real eruptions by watching which part of the plumbing is behaving how.

body.heading: Think and talk
paragraphs: 1. In the model, what plays the part of the gas pressure in a real volcano? What plays the part of magma?
2. Why do you think real volcanoes are cone-shaped mountains, instead of flat cracks in the ground?

takeaway: A volcano is underground plumbing — magma chamber, vent and crater — and eruptions happen when gas pressure drives molten rock up the pipe and out; the model copies that journey with fizz.
materials: Plastic bottle (cut down by a grown-up)
Cardboard, clay or damp sand (the cone)
Warm water, bicarbonate of soda, vinegar, washing-up liquid (grown-up handles)
supervision: A grown-up cuts the bottle, runs all eruption steps (warm water, soda, vinegar), and supervises from build to clean-up.
safetyNotes: Eruptions are a grown-up's job: they pour the vinegar and warm water, and everyone else watches from a step back — foam in eyes stings, so no faces over the crater, ever.
Warm water means warm, never boiling, and only from a grown-up's hands; the model erupts on a tray outdoors or on a washable surface.

The eruption mixture is not food or drink: hands are washed after the build, and leftover mixture is poured away by a grown-up — bicarbonate and vinegar live in the kitchen but this mix belongs to the volcano.
